blocks.text: Move object creation into one overridable or injectable method, so the code that uses the product never names its concrete class.

A **creator** declares a **factory method** that returns a product interface and calls it inside its own algorithm. Subclasses (or an injected `Supplier`) decide which concrete product comes back. The creator's logic stays identical for every product.

items: **Stays stable:** the algorithm that consumes the product.
**Chosen by:** a subclass, a supplier, or a parameter.

blocks.text: Not the same as a static factory such as `List.of`. The GoF pattern is about a polymorphic creation step inside a larger operation.

walkthrough.note: The product interface and two concrete products. The creator will only ever see `Sink`, never `CsvSink` or `JsonSink`.
`createSink()` is the factory method. `render` is the stable algorithm that calls it, so it is `final`. `using` shows the same seam filled by a `Supplier`.
Each concrete creator overrides one method and returns its product. Adding a format means one new pair of classes.
The client holds `Report` references. The same `render` call yields CSV or JSON depending only on the creator it was handed.
When subclassing is heavy, a constructor reference is a complete factory method. This is the form you meet most often in modern code.

blocks.text: A file-ingestion service that supports many vendor formats.

Every vendor sends data in its own format, but the job is always the same: open the file, read records, validate, load. An abstract `ImportJob` owns that sequence and declares `createParser(InputStream)`. `AcmeImport` and `GlobexImport` return their own parsers. Tests subclass the job and return a parser that yields canned records, so no real file is needed.

lists.title: Use when
items: A framework algorithm must create objects whose type only the user code knows.
Tests need to substitute a fake product without touching the algorithm.
Creation needs a name or hook point, such as pooling or logging.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A plain constructor call is enough and the type will not vary.
Subclassing just to change one `new` forces a hierarchy on you.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Calling an overridable factory method from a constructor sees a half-initialized subclass.
A parameterized factory with a `switch` on a string slowly re-creates the coupling.
Returning `null` instead of failing for unknown input.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A creator hierarchy that mirrors the product hierarchy one to one with no shared algorithm.
A `FooFactory` with one method and one implementation.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: A `Supplier<T>` or constructor reference replaces most subclass-based creators.
Sealed interfaces plus a `switch` expression are enough for a closed set of products.

rows.difference: Abstract Factory is a separate object, passed to the client, whose several creation methods keep a product family consistent. Factory Method is one overridable hook inside the creator's own algorithm.
A factory method is typically one step inside a Template Method. The template fixes the sequence; the factory method supplies the object.
Builder assembles one complex object in steps and validates it at the end. Factory Method only decides which class to instantiate.
Prototype creates by copying a configured instance and needs no creator subclasses. Factory Method creates by calling a constructor chosen polymorphically.
Strategy picks behavior to run. Factory Method picks an object to build, and the object is then used however the creator likes.

exercises.scenario: A message-processing framework runs a fixed loop: poll, decode, handle, acknowledge. Each application needs its own decoder class, which only the application knows how to build, and tests want a fake decoder.

options.why: The loop is fixed and one creation step is deferred to the application, which can be overridden or injected in tests.
Only one kind of object is needed. A factory of families adds interfaces with nothing to keep consistent.
The decoders are not copies of configured instances; they are constructed fresh by application code.
Nothing says there must be exactly one decoder, and a global instance would hurt the tests that need a fake.

exercises.prompt: Explain Factory Method in your own words: what is deferred, who decides, and how it differs from Abstract Factory.

modelAnswer.text: A class runs a fixed algorithm but defers one creation step to an overridable or injected method. Subclasses or a supplier decide the concrete product, and the algorithm only sees the interface. Abstract Factory differs: it groups several creation methods to keep a whole family of products consistent.

keyPoints: One creation step is deferred inside a larger algorithm
The creator depends only on the product interface
Subclass override or an injected `Supplier` picks the class
Abstract Factory produces consistent families, not one product
Never call the overridable method from a constructor
